```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, dpi = 96, fig.retina = 1, out.width = "100%"
)
has_glmnet <- requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE)
```

When the outcome is the time to an event, such as death, graft failure, or a hospitalization, pprof
profiles providers with Cox proportional hazards models. This vignette goes through an analysis of
simulated survival data: the data, the model stratified by provider, standardized ratios, tests and
flags, and plots, then recurrent events, competing risks, and penalized models, and last how the
results relate to those of survival's `coxph()` with its defaults. The models follow the definitions
of pprof_py 0.7.0, the group's Python package, and their estimation is done by the survival package,
and by glmnet for penalized models. `vignette("statistical-methods", package = "pprof")` gives the
formulas, and `vignette("models", package = "pprof")` compares the models.

## The data

The patients, their hospitals, and their five risk factors are those of `ExampleDataBinary`. Their
times are simulated here, in days, from a Cox model in which each hospital has its own effect on the
hazard of death; a quarter of the patients enter follow-up late, a transplant ends the follow-up of
others, and follow-up ends after six months to three years.

```{r data, message = FALSE}
library(pprof)
data(ExampleDataBinary)
set.seed(2026)
patients <- data.frame(patient = seq_along(ExampleDataBinary$Y), hospital = ExampleDataBinary$ProvID,
                       ExampleDataBinary$Z)
n <- nrow(patients)
hospital_effect <- rnorm(100, 0, 0.2)[patients$hospital]
risk <- with(patients, 0.4 * z1 - 0.3 * z2 + 0.2 * z3)
patients$entry <- ifelse(runif(n) < 0.25, sample(1:180, n, replace = TRUE), 0)
end <- patients$entry + sample(180:1095, n, replace = TRUE)
death <- patients$entry + ceiling(rexp(n, exp(risk + hospital_effect) / 1500))
transplant <- patients$entry + ceiling(rexp(n, exp(-0.3 * patients$z1) / 2500))
patients$exit <- pmin(death, transplant, end)
patients$status <- factor(ifelse(patients$exit == end & end < pmin(death, transplant), "censored",
                                 ifelse(death <= transplant, "death", "transplant")),
                          levels = c("censored", "death", "transplant"))
patients$died <- as.integer(patients$status == "death")
head(patients)
```

```{r data-facts, include = FALSE}
counts <- table(patients$status)
```

`patients` holds `r format(nrow(patients), big.mark = ",")` patients of
`r length(unique(patients$hospital))` hospitals. A patient is at risk from `entry` to `exit` (in days
since a common origin, such as the start of treatment), and `died` records whether follow-up ended in
death: `r format(counts[["death"]], big.mark = ",")` deaths,
`r format(counts[["transplant"]], big.mark = ",")` transplants, and `r format(counts[["censored"]], big.mark = ",")`
patients whose follow-up ended otherwise. A patient who enters late is not at risk before the entry
day: `Surv(entry, exit, died)` gives each patient's interval (entry, exit], and a right-censored
response without late entries is written `Surv(exit, died)`.

Times are compared exactly. survival's `coxph()` by default merges times that differ only by
rounding (its `timefix`), while pprof, like pprof_py, does not. Times in whole units, such as days,
avoid the question; `check_data()` reports the times that `coxph()`'s default would merge, along with
the other problems a Cox fit can have:

```{r check}
check_data(Surv(entry, exit, died) ~ z1 + z2 + z3, patients, provider = "hospital")
```

## The model stratified by provider

`fit_cox_stratified()` fits the Cox model with a baseline hazard of its own for each hospital and
coefficients shared by all, λ~ij~(t) = λ~0i~(t) exp(z~ij~'β), by maximizing the partial likelihood
stratified by hospital. The hospitals' differences are left in their baseline hazards rather than
estimated as effects: profiling then compares each hospital's observed events with those expected
for its patients (He and Schaubel 2014).

```{r fit}
fit <- fit_cox_stratified(Surv(entry, exit, died) ~ z1 + z2 + z3, data = patients, provider = "hospital")
fit
summary(fit)
```

Tied event times are handled by Breslow's method by default (Breslow 1974), or by Efron's with
`ties = "efron"` (Efron 1977). `robust = TRUE`, or a `cluster` column, gives the robust variance of Lin
and Wei (1989), and `weights` case weights. The fit is survival's: the same model from `coxph()`,
with the settings pprof passes, gives the same coefficients, and its defaults give others.

```{r coxph}
same <- survival::coxph(Surv(entry, exit, died) ~ z1 + z2 + z3 + strata(hospital), data = patients,
                        ties = "breslow", timefix = FALSE)
identical(unname(coef(fit)), unname(coef(same)))
defaults <- survival::coxph(Surv(entry, exit, died) ~ z1 + z2 + z3 + strata(hospital), data = patients)
max(abs(coef(fit) - coef(defaults)))
```

`baseline_hazard()` gives each hospital's baseline cumulative hazard, at covariates 0, and
`predict()` the cumulative hazards and survival curves of new patients; both need the data, kept
with `keep_data = TRUE` or passed again:

```{r baseline}
head(baseline_hazard(fit, data = patients))
```

## Standardized ratios

`standardize_providers()` compares each hospital's observed deaths O~i~ with the deaths E~i~ expected
for its patients:

```{r measures}
measures <- standardize_providers(fit, standardization = c("indirect", "direct"))
head(measures$table)
```

E~i~ sums, over the hospital's patients, the national baseline hazard over each patient's time at
risk, times the patient's relative risk exp(z~ij~'β̂). The national baseline is the Breslow estimator
over all hospitals' patients at the fitted coefficients, so that the expected deaths of all
hospitals add up to the deaths observed. The indirect ratio O~i~ / E~i~, the standardized mortality
ratio (SMR) when the event is death, is above 1 when a hospital has more deaths than expected for its
patients. The direct ratio puts every hospital on the same patients: the deaths the whole population
would have at hospital i's own baseline hazard, estimated from its patients, over the deaths the
population has. `provider_table(fit)` gives each hospital's events and person-time, the sum of its
patients' times at risk.

The expected deaths count every patient, also those with a case weight of 0, without weights, and use
Breslow's estimator whatever the ties of the fit, as pprof_py's measures do. A hospital none of whose
patients is at risk at any time of death has no expected deaths; its ratio is undefined or infinite,
with a warning.

## Tests and flags

`test_providers()` tests each hospital's ratio against 1 and flags it as higher (1) or lower (-1) than
expected, or as expected (0). Under the null hypothesis the hospital's number of deaths is taken to
be Poisson with mean E~i~. The default test is the mid-p test, which counts half the probability of
the observed count (Lancaster 1961); the exact test, `test = "exact"`, counts all of it and is the
more conservative of the two.

```{r tests}
tests <- test_providers(fit)
table(tests$table$flag)
exact <- test_providers(fit, test = "exact")
table(exact$table$flag)
```

```{r tests-facts, include = FALSE}
flags <- table(factor(tests$table$flag, levels = -1:1))
```

At level 0.95 the mid-p test flags `r flags[["1"]]` hospitals as higher and `r flags[["-1"]]` as lower
than expected. Each hospital is tested at that level without an adjustment for multiple testing, so
that about 1 in 20 of the hospitals with no difference from the norm are flagged by chance, as
`vignette("pprof", package = "pprof")` explains. The tests are two-sided.

`interval = "midp"` or `"exact"` adds the limits of the indirect ratio that invert each test; the
exact limits are Garwood's (1936) when E~i~ is below 100 and Byar's approximation otherwise:

```{r intervals}
intervals <- standardize_providers(fit, interval = "midp")
head(intervals$table)
```

## Plots

A funnel plot shows each hospital's indirect ratio against its expected deaths, with the limits of
the mid-p test at each expected count, so that a hospital lies outside the limits exactly when the
test flags it:

```{r funnel}
plot_funnel(funnel_limits(fit, level = c(0.95, 0.998)))
```

A caterpillar plot shows the ratios with their intervals:

```{r caterpillar}
plot_caterpillar(intervals, use_flag = TRUE)
```

`plot_volume()` plots the ratios against each hospital's number of rows of data. With one row per
patient, as here, that is its number of patients; with several rows per patient, as in the next
section, it is not, and the funnel plot, which uses the expected events, is the better guide to how
precise each ratio is.

## Recurrent events

When patients can have the event more than once, as with hospitalizations, each patient's follow-up
is split into intervals that end at each event, `Surv(start, stop, event)`, and the robust variance,
clustered by patient, allows for the dependence between a patient's events (Andersen and Gill 1982;
Lin, Wei, Yang and Ying 2000). Here the hospitalizations of each patient are simulated during the
patient's follow-up:

```{r recurrent}
set.seed(2027)
rate <- exp(0.3 * patients$z1 + 0.2 * patients$z4) / 400
days <- patients$entry + t(apply(matrix(ceiling(rexp(n * 30, rate)), n), 1, cumsum))
during <- days < patients$exit
patient <- c(row(days)[during], seq_len(n))
ends <- c(days[during], patients$exit)
hospitalized <- c(rep(1L, sum(during)), rep(0L, n))
sorted <- order(patient, ends)
hospitalizations <- data.frame(patient = patient[sorted], stop = ends[sorted], hospitalized = hospitalized[sorted])
# Each interval starts where the patient's previous one stopped, the first at the patient's entry.
first <- !duplicated(hospitalizations$patient)
hospitalizations$start <- c(NA, hospitalizations$stop[-nrow(hospitalizations)])
hospitalizations$start[first] <- patients$entry[hospitalizations$patient[first]]
hospitalizations$hospital <- patients$hospital[hospitalizations$patient]
hospitalizations$z1 <- patients$z1[hospitalizations$patient]
hospitalizations$z4 <- patients$z4[hospitalizations$patient]
recurrent <- fit_cox_stratified(Surv(start, stop, hospitalized) ~ z1 + z4, hospitalizations,
                                provider = "hospital", cluster = "patient")
recurrent
shr <- standardize_providers(recurrent)
head(shr$table)
```

The ratio of observed to expected hospitalizations is a standardized hospitalization ratio (SHR).
These ratios are He and Schaubel's measures, as in pprof_py; measures used in public reporting, such
as a standardized hospitalization ratio of dialysis facilities, may be defined otherwise.

## Competing risks

A transplant ends a patient's follow-up before death can occur. The model above treats it as
censoring: its coefficients and ratios describe the hazard of death, which is the cause-specific
model of death. Writing the event of interest in `Surv()` gives the cause-specific model of any event
type, and profiling works on it as on any stratified fit:

```{r cause-specific}
transplants <- fit_cox_stratified(Surv(entry, exit, status == "transplant") ~ z1 + z2 + z3, patients,
                                  provider = "hospital")
coef(transplants)
head(standardize_providers(transplants)$table, 3)
```

The Fine-Gray model describes instead the cumulative incidence of death, the probability of dying
by a given time when transplants compete with death (Fine and Gray 1999): patients with a transplant
stay in the risk set, with weights that decrease over time. `fit_fine_gray()` fits it stratified by
hospital, with survival's `finegray()` and a weighted Cox fit whose variance is robust, clustered by
patient; `cause` names the event of interest, and `id` the patient of each row:

```{r fine-gray}
fine_gray <- fit_fine_gray(Surv(entry, exit, status) ~ z1 + z2 + z3, patients, provider = "hospital",
                           cause = "death", id = "patient")
summary(fine_gray)
curves <- predict(fine_gray, newdata = data.frame(z1 = c(-1, 1), z2 = 0, z3 = 0, hospital = 1),
                  type = "cumulative_incidence", data = patients)
# The cumulative incidence of death after one and two years in hospital 1, for z1 = -1 and z1 = 1.
at <- function(days) {
  sapply(split(curves, curves$row), function(k) k$cumulative_incidence[max(which(k$time <= days))])
}
incidence <- rbind(one_year = at(365), two_years = at(730))
colnames(incidence) <- c("z1 = -1", "z1 = 1")
incidence
```

The two models answer different questions: the cause-specific hazard describes the rate of death
among the patients still at risk, and the subdistribution hazard of the Fine-Gray model the
cumulative incidence of death (Putter, Fiocco and Geskus 2007). The Fine-Gray model has no provider
measures: ratios built on the subdistribution hazard would be a new method, so the profiling
functions raise an error for it.

## Penalized models

`fit_cox_penalized()` fits the Cox model stratified by provider with an elastic-net penalty on the
coefficients, over a decreasing sequence of penalties λ, and `select_lambda()` chooses λ by
cross-validation (Simon, Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani 2011). The paths are computed by glmnet,
a suggested package; the code below runs only when glmnet is installed.

```{r penalized, eval = has_glmnet}
path <- fit_cox_penalized(Surv(entry, exit, died) ~ z1 + z2 + z3 + z4 + z5, patients, provider = "hospital",
                          n_lambda = 20)
set.seed(1)
selected <- select_lambda(path, n_folds = 5, data = patients)
selected$selected
tidy(selected)
```

`alpha` sets the mix of the lasso (`alpha = 1`, the default) and ridge (`alpha = 0`) penalties, and
`penalty_factor` leaves chosen covariates unpenalized. The penalties, the cross-validation's
deviance, and its folds are those of pprof_py, as the next section says. A penalized fit has no
standard errors and no provider profiling, so those functions raise an error for it.

## pprof and the defaults of `coxph()`

pprof's Cox models reproduce pprof_py's results, computed by survival and glmnet, where survival's
own defaults would differ:

| | pprof | survival's `coxph()` |
|---|---|---|
| Tied event times | Breslow's method; Efron's with `ties = "efron"` | Efron's method |
| Times that differ by rounding | compared exactly | merged (`timefix = TRUE`) |
| Robust variance | with `robust = TRUE` or a `cluster` column | also turned on by a `cluster()` term or non-integer weights |
| Case weights of 0 | the rows are left out of the fit and kept in the measures | an error |
| Covariates the fit cannot estimate, or no events | an error that names them | missing coefficients |
| The reported baseline hazard | at covariates 0 and offset 0 | `basehaz()`: at the covariates' means by default |
| Missing values | the rows are dropped | the rows are dropped |

The expected events of the measures count every row without weights, at Breslow's estimator of the
national baseline whatever the fit's ties. The penalized models compute their penalties as pprof_py
does, from the smallest that sets every penalized coefficient to 0 down to a fraction of it, and pass
them to glmnet. `select_lambda()` fits every fold on the whole data's penalties and normalizes each
fold's deviance by the weight of its held-out events, as pprof_py does and as glmnet's `cv.glmnet()`
did before glmnet 5, which normalizes by the held-out weight; its folds spread the events evenly, and
are drawn with R's random numbers, so that they differ from pprof_py's for the same seed.
